title: Centrifugal Force
short_intro: Centrifugal force is an inertial or pseudo-force experienced by bodies in a non-inertial rotating reference frame, directed radially outward from the axis of rotation. It arises purely as a consequence of the acceleration of the coordinate system rather than any physical interaction between masses.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of centrifugal force, distinction between inertial and rotating frames, magnitude mω<sup>2</sup>r, simple numericals on revolving bodies, and effect of Earth's rotation on apparent weight.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed transformation of coordinates from an inertial to a rotating frame, derivation of fictitious forces including centrifugal and Coriolis forces, and latitudinal variation of acceleration due to gravity.

prerequisites: Newton's Laws of Motion in inertial frames
Kinematics of circular motion and angular velocity vector ω
Centripetal acceleration and non-inertial reference frames

concept_notes.heading: Nature of Centrifugal Force
bullets: It is a fictitious or pseudo-force that appears only when observations are made from a non-inertial rotating frame of reference.
It has no physical origin in terms of fundamental interactions (like gravitational or electromagnetic forces); no reaction pair exists in an inertial frame.
Its magnitude is given by F<sub>cf</sub> = mω<sup>2</sup>r, where r is the perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation.

concept_notes.heading: Direction and Vector Form
bullets: The centrifugal force is directed radially outward, away from the instantaneous center of rotation or axis of rotation.
In vector notation, it is expressed as F<sub>cf</sub> = -m(ω × (ω × r)), which simplifies to mω<sup>2</sup>r<sub>⊥</sub> directed outward.
It acts along the line extending from the rotation axis through the position of the particle.

concept_notes.heading: Centrifugal vs Centripetal Force
bullets: Centripetal force is a real inward force (tension, gravity, normal force) required to keep a body moving in a curved path in an inertial frame.
Centrifugal force is directed outward and is utilized in rotating frames to apply D'Alembert's principle, treating equilibrium problems dynamically.
In a rotating frame, the real centripetal force is balanced by the centrifugal force, giving a net zero acceleration in that frame.

concept_notes.heading: Effect of Earth's Rotation on Gravity
bullets: Earth is a non-inertial rotating frame with angular speed ω ≈ 7.29 × 10<sup>-5</sup> rad/s.
Objects on Earth's surface experience a centrifugal force outward perpendicular to the polar axis, reducing the effective gravitational force.
The effective acceleration due to gravity g' varies with latitude λ, being minimum at the equator and maximum at the poles.

derivations.title: Derivation of Centrifugal Force from Rotating Reference Frame Transformation
derivations.conditions: A coordinate system S' rotating with uniform angular velocity ω relative to an inertial frame S.
steps: Express the position vector in terms of unit vectors of the rotating frame: r = x'î' + y'&jhat;' + z'&khat;'.
Take the time derivative in the inertial frame noting that unit vectors change with time: (dî'/dt) = ω × î'.
Apply the operator relation (d/dt)<sub>inertial</sub> = (d/dt)<sub>rotating</sub> + ω × to velocity and then to acceleration.
Equate m a<sub>inertial</sub> = F<sub>real</sub> and isolate the apparent acceleration in the rotating frame: a<sub>rot</sub> = (F<sub>real</sub>/m) - 2(ω × v<sub>rot</sub>) - ω × (ω × r).
Identify the term -m(ω × (ω × r)) as the centrifugal force.

derivations.title: Variation of Effective Acceleration Due to Gravity with Latitude
derivations.conditions: Earth modeled as a sphere of radius R rotating with angular velocity ω at latitude λ.
steps: Consider a body of mass m at latitude λ. The distance from the axis of rotation is r = R cosλ.
The centrifugal force acting on the body is outward along the radius of the circular path, with magnitude F<sub>c</sub> = mω<sup>2</sup>(R cosλ).
The true gravitational force mg acts toward the center of the Earth.
Resolve the centrifugal force into components: mg<sub>c</sub>cosλ radially inward and mg<sub>c</sub>sinλ tangentially.
Write the net effective weight mg' vector sum: g' = g - ω<sup>2</sup>R cos<sup>2</sup>λ (using scalar approximation for small corrections).

solved_numericals.question: A mass of 2 kg is tied to a string of length 0.5 m and rotated in a horizontal circle at 120 revolutions per minute. Calculate the centrifugal force acting on the mass in the rotating frame.
solution_steps: Convert RPM to angular velocity: ω = (2 π × 120)/60 = 4π rad/s ≈ 12.566 rad/s.
Identify given values: m = 2 kg, r = 0.5 m.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the angular speed with which the Earth must rotate on its axis so that a person at the equator weighs three-fifths of their normal weight. Take g = 10 m/s<sup>2</sup> and Earth's radius R = 6400 km.
solution_steps: At the equator, effective weight is given by mg' = mg - mω<sup>2</sup>R.
Given condition: mg' = (3/5)mg, which implies mω<sup>2</sup>R = mg - (3/5)mg = (2/5)mg.
Cancel mass m and solve for ω: ω<sup>2</sup>R = (2/5)g ⇒ ω = sqrt(2g / (5R)).
Substitute values: g = 10 m/s<sup>2</sup>, R = 6400 km = 6.4 × 10<sup>6</sup> m.

solved_numericals.question: A smooth horizontal disc rotates with a constant angular velocity ω about a vertical axis passing through its center. A small particle of mass m is placed on the disc at a distance r from the axis. What is the time taken by the particle to slide off the edge if the radius of the disc is R and the coefficient of static friction is μ? Assume initial velocity is zero relative to the disc.
solution_steps: In the rotating frame of the disc, the forces acting on the particle are centrifugal force (mω<sup>2</sup>r) radially outward and maximum static friction (μmg) radially inward.

The particle begins to slide when centrifugal force exceeds maximum static friction: mω<sup>2</sup>r > μmg, or at any position r, the radial equation of motion in the rotating frame is m(d<sup>2</sup>r/dt<sup>2</sup>) = mω<sup>2</sup>r - μmg (assuming sliding has commenced with kinetic friction μ<sub>k</sub>, or pure outward acceleration if friction is overcome).
For threshold of sliding starting from r = r<sub>0</sub> where μmg = mω<sup>2</sup>r<sub>0</sub>, r<sub>0</sub> = μg / ω<sup>2</sup>.
If placed at r = 0, friction holds it until mω<sup>2</sup>r = μmg. For purely outward radial motion once sliding starts with negligible friction: d<sup>2</sup>r/dt<sup>2</sup> - ω<sup>2</sup>r = 0.
Solving the differential equation r(t) = A e<sup>ωt</sup> + B e<sup>-\omega t<sup> with initial conditions r(0) = r<sub>0</sub> and dr/dt(0) = 0 yields the transit time to reach R.

assumptions_and_limitations: Centrifugal force applies strictly within non-inertial rotating frames of reference.
The angular velocity ω is assumed uniform unless time-varying pseudo-forces (Euler force) are included.
In geophysical applications, Earth is assumed to be a rigid, spherically symmetric rotating body.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Centrifugal force is the reaction force to centripetal force according to Newton's Third Law.
common_misconceptions.correct: Centripetal and centrifugal forces do not form a Newton's third law action-reaction pair because they act on the same body and belong to different reference frames.
common_misconceptions.why: Action-reaction pairs must act on two different bodies and be of the same physical nature.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Centrifugal force pulls objects outward in an inertial reference frame.
common_misconceptions.correct: Centrifugal force does not exist in an inertial frame of reference; objects simply tend to move in a straight line due to inertia (Newton's first law).
common_misconceptions.why: Pseudo-forces only emerge when mathematical transformations are made to a non-inertial frame.

quick_revision: Centrifugal force is a fictitious outward radial force equal to mω<sup>2</sup>r present in rotating frames.
Magnitude of Centrifugal Force: F_{cf} = m \omega^2 r
Vector Expression for Centrifugal Force: F_{cf} = -m \omega \times (\omega \times r)
